📖 Core Definitions

Essential Terminology & Concepts

Problem Formulation Key Concept

The structures of state space are trees and graphs.

📌 Key Takeaways

Section-by-Section Study Breakdown

2.2.1 Problem Formulation

  • The structures of state space are trees and graphs.
  • A tree has one and only one path from any point to any other point.
  • Graph consists of a set of nodes (vertices) and a set of edges (arcs).
  • Arcs establish relationship (connections) between the nodes, i.e., a graph has several paths to a given node.

2.2.2 Structure of a State space

  • In a state space, a solution is a path from the initial state to a goal state or sometime just a goal state.
  • It also gives the cost of applying the operators to the states.
  • A path cost function is used to measure the quality of solution and out of all possible solutions, an optimal solution has the lowest path cost.
  • The importance of cost depends on the problem and the type of solution asked.

2.2.3 Problem solution of State space

  • Many problems can be represented as state space.
  • The state space of a problem includes: an initial state, one or more goal state, set of state transition operator (or a set of production rules), used to change the current state to another state.
  • A control strategy is used that specifies the order in which the rules will be applied.
  • For example, Depth-first search (DFS), Breath-first search (BFS) etc.

2.3.4 Searching for solution in state spaces formulated

  • Establishes essential concepts, mathematical or computational foundations, and techniques of searching for solution in state spaces formulated.
  • Applies standard methodologies relevant to modern data science workflows and analysis in problem solving using search.

2.3 Formulation of 8 puzzle problem from AI perspective

  • The eight-tile puzzle consists of a 3-by-3 (3×3) square frame board which holds eight (8) movable tiles numbered as 1 to 8.
  • One square is empty, allowing the adjacent tiles to be shifted.
  • There are 4 operators that is, “Moving the blank”: Move the blank UP, Move the blank DOWN, Move the blank LEFT and Move the blank RIGHT.
  • Here cost of each action (blank move) = 1, so cost of a sequence of actions= the number of actions.

2.4 N-queen’s problem- Formulation and Solution

  • The N-Queen problem is the problem of placing N Queen’s (Q1,Q2,Q3,….
  • Qn) on an N×N chessboard so that no two queens attack each other.
  • The colour of the queens is meaningless in this puzzle, and any queen is assumed to be attack any other.
  • So, a solution requires that no two queens share the same row, column, or diagonal.

2.4.1 Formulation of 8 Queen’s problem

  • States: any arrangement of 0 to 4 queens on the board Initial state: 0 queens on the board Successor function: Add queen in any square Goal test: 4 queens on the board, none attacked For the initial state, there are 16 successors.
  • At the next level, each of the states has 15 successors, and so on down the line.
  • This search tree can be restricted by considering only those successors where No queens are attacking each other.
  • To do that, we have to check the new queen with all the other queens on the board.

2.4.2 State space tree for 4-Queen’s problem

  • We place queen row-by-row (i.e.,Q_1in row 1, Q_2 in row 2 and so on).
  • If you want optimal solution, then go for Dynamic programming.
  • In a tree, the value (i,j) means in thei^(th )row, j^th queen is placed.
  • Edges from level 1 to level 2 nodes specify the values for x1.
